entries.finding: A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis included 70 randomized controlled trials of prebiotics, probiotics, or synbiotics for adult depressive or anxiety symptoms, with interventions lasting 2 to 24 weeks.
Pre-/pro-/synbiotic supplementation reduced depressive symptoms with a pooled SMD of -0.57 (95% CI -0.71 to -0.43; p<0.001), but heterogeneity was substantial (I²=83.0%).
Pre-/pro-/synbiotic supplementation reduced anxiety symptoms with a pooled SMD of -0.43 (95% CI -0.59 to -0.28; p<0.001), with substantial heterogeneity (I²=80.5%).

For depression, probiotics and synbiotics showed significant pooled effects while prebiotics did not; for anxiety, all three intervention classes showed significant pooled effects, with synbiotics having the largest subgroup estimate.

The review judged the evidence limited by substantial heterogeneity and overall moderate methodological quality and explicitly framed pre-/pro-/synbiotics as adjunctive options rather than replacements for standard evidence-based depression or anxiety treatments.

An updated 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis included 39 randomized placebo-controlled trials with 4,094 participants evaluating probiotic supplementation and subjective or objective sleep outcomes.
Probiotics improved global Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores by a pooled MD of -0.71 (95% CI -1.23 to -0.20), but the certainty of evidence was rated very low.

Selected PSQI domains improved with probiotics, including daytime dysfunction (MD -0.08; 95% CI -0.11 to -0.05) and sleep time (MD 0.11; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.21), while other subdomains did not show consistent effects.

Overall insomnia severity did not significantly improve (SMD 0.17; 95% CI -1.15 to 1.49); a sensitivity analysis excluding one influential study produced SMD -0.44 (95% CI -0.74 to -0.14) with low-certainty evidence.

Objective outcomes showed modest changes, including 13.82 additional minutes of total sleep time (95% CI 1.15 to 26.49) and 5.15 fewer minutes awake during the sleep period (95% CI 0.43 to 9.87); the authors noted generally low certainty and uncertain clinical meaningfulness.
A 2025 systematic review identified 30 randomized controlled trials of anthocyanin intake and adult cognition or mood; 14 studies with 733 participants met criteria for meta-analysis.
Anthocyanin intake did not significantly improve working memory in pooled analysis (Hedges' g -0.183; 95% CI -0.407 to 0.041; p=0.110).
Anthocyanin intake did not significantly improve verbal learning in pooled analysis (Hedges' g 0.054; 95% CI -0.215 to 0.324; p=0.69).
Anthocyanin intake did not significantly improve immediate memory in pooled analysis (Hedges' g 0.196; 95% CI -0.242 to 0.633; p=0.38).

Although qualitative synthesis reported improvements in several cognitive domains and 4 of 15 studies reported mood benefits, pooled effects for working memory, verbal learning, immediate memory, and delayed memory were not significant; heterogeneity was cited as an important limitation.

A 2026 systematic review included 18 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of orally administered Zingiberaceae-derived interventions such as curcumin, turmeric, and ginger for adult cognitive outcomes.
Zingiberaceae-derived interventions improved pooled memory-related outcomes with an SMD of 0.57 (95% CI 0.13 to 1.02).
No significant pooled effect was observed for executive function and processing speed in the Zingiberaceae cognition meta-analysis.
No significant pooled effects were observed for global cognition or for attention/inhibitory-control outcomes.

The authors characterized the evidence as very uncertain because of substantial heterogeneity, limited study numbers, risk of bias in some trials, and variation in populations, formulations, and cognitive measures.
A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis included eight randomized controlled trials with 594 participants evaluating ginger alone or as an adjunct for acute or preventive migraine treatment.

For acute treatment, one 60-participant study of ginger plus ketoprofen versus placebo plus ketoprofen suggested lower headache severity at two hours (MD -1.27; 95% CI -1.46 to -1.08), but certainty was low.
Evidence was very uncertain for whether ginger plus feverfew versus placebo or ginger alone versus sumatriptan improved pain relief, pain-free response, or two-hour headache severity.

For preventive treatment, ginger added to an active drug reduced headache pain severity at three months versus the same active drug with or without placebo (pooled MD -3.18; 95% CI -3.94 to -2.42; 2 studies, 183 participants), with low-certainty evidence.

Across migraine outcomes, certainty ranged from low to very low; the review concluded that current evidence is too uncertain to establish ginger as effective for either acute or preventive migraine treatment.
